source.title: Inductive Bias of Gradient Descent for Exponentially Weight Normalized Smooth Homogeneous Neural Nets

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is supplied.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports training results on toy and MNIST datasets that bear on training loss reaching very low values and on normalization changing convergence and pruning behavior, using different architectures and objectives than the versions’ main benchmark claims.
record.gate_note: Results include loss convergence for EWN, SWN and unnormalized networks, plus MNIST pruning experiments. The paper does not test CIFAR-10/100, random-label fitting, shortcuts, initialization comparisons, above-stability learning rates, or batch normalization. Reported pruning-accuracy curves and some convergence-rate plots are figure-only; the text states their qualitative comparisons. The paper’s MNIST pruning result measures test accuracy after pruning, so it does not by itself establish training classification error.
record.test_reason: No result tests V1–V6. The experiments use fully connected MNIST networks or toy models, measure sparsity and convergence under weight normalization, and do not compare batch normalization. Random-label fitting is cited to motivate a separability assumption; vanishing loss is assumed for the gradient-descent theory.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase accurately reflects the conclusion, but needs qualification: the faster EWN convergence rates are theoretical results under stated trajectory and learning-rate assumptions. Relative sparsity is supported experimentally, including with ReLU. Appendix O reports slightly faster unnormalized convergence at extremely low MNIST loss under a schedule outside the rate theorem's assumptions. Extending the theory to nonsmooth networks and establishing the trajectory assumptions for weight-normalized networks remain open.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes exponential and standard weight normalization on smooth homogeneous networks using exponential or cross-entropy losses, with toy and MNIST experiments; it does not reproduce the cited benchmark-error recipes in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported behavior varies by parameterization (EWN, SWN, unnormalized), training loss level, dataset and number of layers; pruning results are shown at e−10, e−100 and e−300.

fits_no_version.finding: At sufficiently low training loss, EWN gives better MNIST test accuracy after pruning than SWN or unnormalized networks. The pruning procedure selects the best test-performing strategy at each pruning level.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Exponential weight normalization can improve pruning efficacy in the tested fully connected MNIST networks.

fits_no_version.finding: In the ReLU XOR experiment, EWN asymptotically uses four of twenty neurons; SWN and unnormalized networks use almost all twenty.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Exponential weight normalization favors asymptotic relative neuron sparsity in the tested XOR setup.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing linear-network depth from one to four layers speeds loss convergence under all three parameterizations, with a smaller depth effect under EWN.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The dependence of convergence speed on depth varies with weight parameterization in shallow linear networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix O reports comparable initial MNIST convergence across parameterizations, followed by slightly faster unnormalized training at extremely low loss under the aggressive learning-rate schedule.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: EWN's theoretical asymptotic speed advantage does not establish a speed advantage under every training schedule.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Algorithmic Learning Theory; Proceedings of Machine Learning Research vol 167 (2022)
record.problems: MNIST pruning results are shown as figures without exact values in text and use post-pruning test accuracy rather than training classification error. The MNIST experiment is restricted to two classes for the separate 2-class analysis; the pruning experiment's seed count is described only as multiple seeds. The theoretical conclusions depend on stated trajectory and smoothness assumptions.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible results were left out. Theory statements about loss tending to zero under assumptions are not separate experimental rows; figures 11 and 12 show convergence rates but the text only reports an aggregate qualitative comparison, captured under R8/R9 for the layer-count experiment.

untested.parts: Convolutional CIFAR-10/100 training classification error, random-label fitting, and dependence on capacity, stopping, or regularization.
Teacher-student ReLU local-minimum frequencies and the effect of one or two extra student neurons.
Deep plain convolutional training degradation, identity shortcuts, and the stated initialization alternatives.
Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, and trainable depth.
Learning rates relative to measured stability thresholds, curvature evolution, catapult recovery, and edge-of-stability behavior.
Batch-normalized versus otherwise comparable networks, higher-learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup residual training.

record.verdict_notes: States are cannot_determine relative to V1–V6 because the rows measure other outcomes; this does not dispute the reported sparsity or convergence findings. Extremely small training losses provide fitting evidence for these particular networks, but do not establish V1's specified architecture and dataset claim. Weight normalization is not batch normalization, and aggressive learning rates alone do not establish V5 without a stability-threshold comparison.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/100, random or corrupted labels, SGD/Adam comparisons, smaller-model and early-stopping effects. The MNIST experiments report loss and post-pruning test accuracy, not training classification error.

rows.note: This is post-pruning test accuracy, not training classification error. The text says EWN outperforms SWN and unnormalized networks when loss is sufficiently low, without identifying this panel’s exact comparison in text.
rows.check: Post-pruning test accuracy in a fully connected MNIST network does not measure V1's training classification error in convolutional CIFAR networks. The loss level is a pruning checkpoint.
